Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II, EDSA car. Mapagrnahal St., Dilirnan, Quezon City OFFICE OF THE SECI*TARY OILG OPINION NO. 9 S. I O February 2005 MS. EULALIA T. TAIARAN Accountant IV, OIC Office of the Provincial Accountant Provincial Capitol Building Virac, Catanduanes Dear Ms. Talaran: This pertains to your letter seeking our legal opinion relative to the legality of a Budget Ordinance allegedly passed and approved by only four (4) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Catanduanes through a special session. Per your letter, the Budget Ordinance was passed and approved by four (4) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Catanduanes through a special session held on 13 March 2004, while the seven (7) other members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan were in Manila for a luncheon meeting with Her Excellency, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo. You further represented that the seven (7) members have no approved travel orders from the Office of the Qovemor. May we, however, note that in one of your attachments (Resolution No. 029-2004), it appears that there were eight (8) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan, including the Vice-Governor, and not seven (7), per your letter, who were not in the province on the day when the assailed special session was conducted by the remaining four (4) members of the said sanggunian. Be that as it may, please be informed that the passage of an ordinance involves two (2) aspects, i.e. (I) the substantive; and (2) the procedural. 'Ihe former refers to the necessity of an ordinance to comply with the provisions of the Local Govemment Code of 1991 (RA 7160), other existing laws and the Constitution. The latter, in the meantime, refers to the manner by which an ordinance has to be enacted. Any violation of these two (2) aspects may render an ordinance invalid. As regards the substantive aspect, the same involves a question of law which may be validly addressed through the rendition of a legal opinion, as the latter entails only an interpretation of the provisions of the ordinance vis-å-vis the laws and Constitution whereupon said ordinance should be compliant with. Insofar as the procedural aspect is concemed, let it be stressed that this aspect usually involves more of questions of fact, because

-2- It involves the contemporaneous events that surrounded the procedure/manner of the passage of the ordinance. Sometimes, a necessity of factual detennination as to the proper procedure undertaken in the passage of a particular ordinance would become imperative If the matter is timely raised by any proper party. In such a case, the aid of the court to resolve the issue has to be implored since this Department, not being a court, is not empowered to adjudicate factual issues. Be that as it may, for whatever guidance it may serve, we wish to inform you that in Qamboa, Jr. vs. Aguirre Jr., 310 SCRA 867, the Supreme Court here resolved that a mayor who was out of the country is considered •effectively absent" as he cannot exercise the powers and prerogaüves of his office abroad. This also creates a temporary vacancy in the office of the mayor and the vice-mayor is allowed to discharge the duties of the mayor during the latter's absence. While admittedly in Qamboa, Jn vse Aguirre Jr., supra, the mayor was abroad, in the case of Paredes vs. Antillon, 3 SCRA 662, the Supreme Court had a chance to pass upon the prior case of Qrapilon vs. Municipality of CarÜra, Leyte, Q.R. No. L-12347, 30 May 1961, wherein a Leyte mayor traveled to Manila: to transact official business. The Coun resolved that a mayor traveling within the Philippines but outside the territorial jurisdicåon of his municipality is considered as not being effectively absent if the travel is official because he can still exercise the powers and prerogatives of his office. The reverse should necessarily be true. If the travel outside of his local government unit is unofficial or private, the traveling local chief executive is deemed to be effectively absent because he cannot exercise the powers and prerogatives of his office precisely due to the private nature of his travel. In this specific case, the powers and prerogatives of his office remain within the territorial bounds of his local government unit. Moreover, in Avelino vs. Cuenco (83 Phil. 17), the Supreme Court excluded a Member of the Senate in the determination of quorum for the reason that said Senator was in the United States and, therefore, outside the coercive jurisdiction of the Senate. Foregoing doctrines considered, this Department through DILQ Opinion No. 27, s. 2004, once opined that if we, were to apply the three (3) Supreme Court doctrines, i.e., Qamboa, Jr. vs. Aguirre, Jr. (310 SCRA 867); Paredes vs. Antillon (3 SCRA 662); and Grapilon vs. Municipality of Carigara, Leyte (2 SCRA 103), an effectively absent member (the City Councilor) "is not considered in the determination of the basis for the quorum of said body" as the travel outside his city which is not on official business may be considered as disabling himself from acting on official and business transactions of his office. Corollary thereto, Section 53 (b) of RA 7160 refers to the power of the Presiding Officer to "compel the immediate attendance of any member absent without justifiable cause by designating a member of the sanggunlan,

-3- to be assisted by a member or members of the police force assigned in the territorial jurisdiction of the local government unit concemed, to arrest the absent member and present him at the session in order to complete the quorum of the leØslative body." However, said coercive jurisdiction of the Vice-Mayor as Presiding Officer of the Sangguniang Panlungsod to require the attendance of an absent councilor seems to only be effective within the territorial jurisdiction of the city as the Local Govemment Code limits the vice-mayor's authority to legally demand assistance from the PNP to effect such arrest to embrace only those police personnel assigned within the boundaries of his city. No such authority to the vice-mayor over the PNP extends beyond the boundaries of his city. Otherwise said, the vice-mayor or the sangguniang panlungsod have no coercive jurisdiction over their sanggunlan members beyond the boundaries of their city if the latter's travel is unofficial. In this regard, when the absent city councilor or any other elected local government official for that matter is privately traveling outside his city within (or outside) the Philippines, he Is effectively absent and/or temporarily incapacitated from acting on the official and business transactions of his office. Henceforth, if we were to apply these Supreme Court doctrines to the Instant case, it would seem that the effective absence of the eight (8) SP Members would result to their exclusion in the determination of quorum. However, while this Depaftment is the executive office tasked with the Interpretation of the Local Qovemment Code of 1991, and therefore, its legal opinion is Wven great weight by the courts, the determination with finality of the applicability or non-applicability of the Supreme Court decisions mentioned above vis-å-vis DILQ Opinion No. 27, s. 2004 to the facts of the Instant case is a matter to be best resolved by our courts of law. It is a well-accepted principle that when there are conflicting claims to a certain issue, courts should step in to resolve the same. In the meantime, we are constrained to adhere to the rule on the presumption of the regularity and validity of the action the concerned Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members have undertaken in the conduct of special session and the enactment of the budget Ordinance pursuant to Rule 131, Section 3 (m) of the Rules of Court of Which we are all bound to adhere. The foregoing, notwithstanding, this Depaftment would like to stress that it sees the wisdom and propriety of the social acceptability of the principles enunciated in the Supreme Court decisions above in connection with the instant matter as it would deter, if not put an end to, the common practice whereby the mqlority members of a sanggunian would resort to the simple expediency of absenting themselves either without justifiable reasons or without approved travel authorities just to hold captive the mlnorlty to the prejudice of the primary functions of their respecUve

-4- sanggunlans. ThiÅ practice would undoubtedly paralyze the plans and programs of the local government unit, to the detriment of their constltuents. We hope that we have guided you accordingly. Very truly yours, ANGEL T.
